detail.abstract:
Inflation has been higher and more volatile in recent years, which makes insurers' claims costs harder to predict. Using euro-area market data for 2008–2025, this paper tests whether investment hedges can protect a stylised European insurer with EUR1 billion of assets. The insurer's claims follow one of four price drivers: consumer prices, motor repairs, construction and medical costs. Each of these four liability types is tested on ten different versions of the insurer's balance sheet. The four types are also combined into ten mixed books of business, such as a motor-led P&C book or a life-and-health book. The paper focuses on the decisions facing asset–liability management (ALM) teams.

Five practical findings emerge.

1. Protection paid off in the inflation surge. A full CPI-swap ladder is a set of inflation swaps sized to offset liabilities indexed to CPI. Such ladders added EUR35–48 million a year to surplus in 2021–23, or 3.5–4.8% of assets, and lost EUR5–11 million a year (0.5–1.1% of assets) outside that episode. Realised CPI contributed about EUR22 million of the annual gain and higher expected inflation the rest. Over the full history the two broadly offset, before trading and collateral costs of about EUR1 million a year (0.1% of assets).

2. Partial hedging is a robust starting point. Half-size ladders reduced surplus variance in every period tested, for each of the four liability types and each of the ten mixed books. For the individual liability types, the reduction was 26–60% during 2021–23 and 4–8% outside it. On nine of the ten mixed books, they covered 47–85% of the inflation-driven rise in liabilities during the surge. They also gave up only half as much in quieter years. There is no stable hedge ratio, so a half ladder is best seen as a starting point to test against the insurer's own book.

3. The right size depends on the liability mix. With hindsight, the ladder size that would have best stabilised surplus ranges from 0.8 times the full ladder for a life-and-health book to 2.1 times for a short-tail P&C book. Without the surge, the range narrows to 0.6–1.1 times. Construction prices overshoot CPI and health prices lag it, and how fully claims follow their price index matters just as much.

4. What is sold to fund the hedge matters. Linkers bought by selling nominal bonds gave lower surplus variance and a better risk–cost score than linkers bought with cash. This held in every period tested on the baseline balance sheet.

5. Diversification is not inflation protection. Healthcare equities diversify the portfolio but protected medical-price exposure only during the surge. Construction equities improved neither measure, and the benefit of commodities depended heavily on the surge.

Under the Solvency II standard formula, CPI swaps barely change required capital. Their value is that they preserve available capital, and hence the solvency ratio, when inflation rises. In the worst year of the surge, a half ladder saved 14–21% of surplus. Ladders added to losses in the 2008 crisis, when equities and inflation expectations fell together. Cash for collateral is the main practical constraint. Insurers should decide hedge size, maturity and funding together, using their own claims history and collateral arrangements.

detail.abstract: Offline retail central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), including the planned offline digital euro, rely on a tamper-resistant secure element (SE) in the holder's device to hold value and prevent double spending. This white paper asks what an issuer can still do when that component fails at scale. Where the validity of offline value rests solely on the integrity of the SE, a batch-wide or low-cost key-recovery flaw in certified hardware, for which there are precedents across vendors, becomes a source of unbacked central bank liabilities that the issuer can neither bound nor attribute. The paper gives an explicit loss model and derives the aggregate detection threshold: unbacked value becomes visible only once the amount already redeemed exceeds the legitimate value held on devices that have not reported, so the privacy of offline holdings and the size of the undetectable fraud budget move together. After detection, every available response, from hardware re-issuance and key rotation to throttling or suspending the offline rail, either leaves the loss open or delivers the disruption a hostile adversary seeks: a self-defense trap. Per-person holding limits do not help, because the same component enforces them. Building on a framework of design axes and privacy properties, the paper adds four containment properties (bounded loss, attribution, quarantine granularity, and detection and revocation latency), assesses five designs against them, and prices an object-centric alternative proposed by the authors, authenticated lineage tokens, in which offline value carries evidence that can be checked independently of the SE, including its data-protection implications. It closes with recommendations on limits, detection, procurement, incident response, loss allocation and identity recovery, set against the state of the digital euro legislation as of October 2026. The analysis is architectural: it tests no product and claims no vulnerability in any deployed or planned device.

detail.abstract: In this study, we adopted the method of Imaginary Future Generations (IFGs), which has been shown to foster "futurability" in people and society, to assess its effectiveness in planning water supply infrastructure through a deliberation experiment involving employees of municipalities in Japan. We conducted a total of five workshops on water infrastructure maintenance and management issues with staff members of the Water Works Bureau of Suita City, Osaka Prefecture. Analysis of workshop discussions from the future (IFG) perspective revealed qualitative changes in discussion contents compared to discussions from the present-day perspective, with a shift in emphasis from cost-effectiveness to future societal conditions. There was also a marked increase in awareness of future risks and crises, such as possible earthquakes, and a tendency to propose new policy directions to address such risks. The results also suggested a tendential shift to proposals and decision-making that give weight to services for future water users while also taking account of the broader operational context, including other service providers. The results of questionnaire surveys 2 of the workshop participants also revealed changes in the relative importance of decision-making criteria when assessing policies. For example, "cost-effectiveness" became less important and the "needs of water users" became more important. Furthermore, the results suggested that the intervention effect of the workshops continued to influence the perceptions of participants beyond the end of the workshops. The insights obtained may help to develop new methodologies for long-term planning and assessment of water infrastructure maintenance and management challenges.

detail.abstract: We studied 1,986 children aged 4-6 years from 1,471 households in the 2023-2024 Nigeria General Household Survey Panel. We compared caregivers' reports of 20 developmental skills with household assets and state-level vegetation greenness, measured using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). The asset score was based on ownership of 41 household goods. Average assigned greenness rose from 0.429 in the lowest asset group to 0.614 in the highest (difference 0.185; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.150-0.220). Children in the highest asset group were more likely to be reported as able to count from 1 to 10 than children in the lowest group (93.3% versus 38.8%); across all 20 skills, nine showed a clear increase with household assets after accounting for multiple comparisons. In the main analysis, children in states with greenness one standard deviation higher had 2.38 times the odds of being reported as able to count from 1 to 10 (95% CI 1.44-3.94). This association was not evident when we used an alternative vegetation measure. A combined score of 19 skills was also higher by 1.47 points for each standard-deviation increase in greenness (95% CI 0.15-2.78; 1,757 children). Maternal education was missing or unknown for 90.2% of children. Overall, higher household assets were linked to greener state surroundings and stronger reports on several skills, while the relationship between greenness and development was less consistent. Because the study compared information collected at one point in time and measured greenness by state, these findings do not establish cause and effect or describe each child's personal exposure.

detail.abstract: We examine how asset embeddings perform in China's A-share market, where investor holdings are of poor quality. To adapt to China, we estimate BERT with a pretrain-finetune paradigm and warm-start its embedding layer from the estimated Word2Vec embeddings. Empirically, we find three new results that are different from or absent in the US market. First, BERT-based asset embeddings perform the best on relative valuation and return comovement at high dimensions and on managed portfolios at every dimension. Second, asset embeddings outperform text embeddings and are more aligned with investor demand, while text embeddings are more aligned with firm industry or name characteristics. Finally, asset embeddings capture the "Chinese characteristics" of the A-share market. They identify state-owned enterprises more accurately than firm characteristics, and their implied state exposures capture incremental information in stock returns beyond the legal SOE label during the 2024Q1 SOE re-rating campaign. A counterfactual experiment supports the rationale for China's hybrid disclosure rule. In general, asset embeddings provide a robust approach to representing a firm beyond traditional observable characteristics.

detail.abstract: Financial intermediation is widely thought to shape innovation, yet most evidence comes from long after the technologies of modern growth were invented. We study this relationship during the Second Industrial Revolution and the decades that followed, when financial institutions expanded rapidly, firms increasingly became corporations, and independent inventors still produced much new technology. Using a new database of narrative accounts of bank distress, we compare counties whose first banking crisis ended in permanent closure with counties that panicked in the same year but kept their bank. Bank closure reduces local patenting by about 4.6 percent over the following twelve years, and the decline grows with the share of the county's banking sector that closed. The effect falls on patents assigned to firms, not on patents held by individual inventors, and on ordinary, not breakthrough, patents.

detail.abstract:
Equity markets have entered a structurally new momentum regime. Price moves of several hundred percent within twelve months no longer occur only in speculative small caps; they now strike decades-old industrial companies, simultaneously, across indices and regions. This paper argues that the trigger varies (artificial intelligence, the geopolitical Zeitenwende, the erosion of trust in the US-led order) while the amplifier remains constant: a market mechanism built from passive capital, options markets, explicit leverage, a growing speculative capital base and a new algorithmic retail layer that transmits and magnifies flows in both directions.

The paper develops the amplifier structure as a three-axes thesis distinguishing the current regime from the dotcom era, proposes a typology of momentum, and discusses the capacity law and alpha decay that constrain any strategy built on it. It tests the amplitude thesis quantitatively: across a universe of roughly 1,000 US large caps (2005 to July 2026) and 166 European names, the share of companies above an inflation-adjusted USD 10 billion threshold with a rolling twelve-month return above +100 percent sits at 1 to 4 percent in quiet years, spikes in the crash rebounds of 2010 and 2021, and in 2024 to 2026 forms the first multi-year rising sequence without a preceding market break in the entire series. The paper treats the antithesis with equal seriousness: the same mechanism that produces amplitude on the way up produces deeper and faster corrections when it breaks, with the momentum crash literature, the absence of safe havens and the geopolitical kill switch examined in turn.

From this follows a practical consequence for portfolio construction: in such a regime a deliberately concentrated vehicle of roughly twenty names can be constructed, and tail-risk hedging has to be rethought as an explicit insurance rather than a daily volatility overlay. The paper closes by framing the regime as a testable hypothesis and naming its own methodological limits. It is the first paper in a series; its downside is developed in the companion paper "The Edge of Tail Risk Catching".

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether population ageing weakens governments' fiscal responsiveness to public debt and whether this relationship differs across economic and political environments. A simple political-economy model with overlapping generations shows that, because older cohorts expect to bear a smaller share of future debt-servicing costs, a rising old-age dependency ratio lowers the equilibrium response of the primary balance to inherited debt. We test this prediction with a fiscal reaction function for 62 advanced and developing economies over 1962–2024. Governments respond positively to rising debt, mainly through primary expenditure, and the response is weaker in more aged societies. With a constant debt coefficient, the ageing effect is imprecisely estimated, but Bayesian panel time-varying-parameter estimates, which absorb common changes in fiscal responsiveness over time, show that ageing clearly dampens the response: moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of the old-age dependency ratio lowers it by about one third. The evidence comes mainly from OECD economies, where ageing is most advanced: the effect is present within the OECD sample, whereas it cannot be identified among non-OECD economies. Time-varying estimates for the components of the primary balance show that ageing weakens the response mainly through the expenditure side: more aged societies cut primary spending by less in response to debt, whereas the response of revenue is unaffected. The dampening effect is also more apparent in democratic economies, consistent with the proposed electoral mechanism.

detail.abstract: Retail crypto trading systems increasingly combine Large Language Models (LLMs) with classical machine learning, yet deployed systems are rarely evaluated with the anti-overfitting discipline that quantitative finance research demands, and LLM-proposed strategy changes are rarely held to out-ofsample evidence before touching real money. We present a production system, operational since October 2026 on the Binance Alpha mid-cap token venue, that (i) combines moving-average rule gates, three LightGBM model families, and a TradingAgents-inspired multi-agent LLM council (Grok for verdicts, Gemini for analysis) in a single advisory-to-execution pipeline; and (ii) wraps every adaptive component in evidence gates: models are promoted only after purged walk-forward exams, LLM-proposed strategy parameter changes must beat the incumbent on an unseen backtest split before automatic deployment, regime-conditional sizing requires a minimum count of demonstrably underperforming trades as evidence, and weekly windows auto-revert losing versions. We report 44 logged model-training runs (including rejected candidates with exam AUC 0.458–0.571), 8 strategy versions with recorded unseen-split races, a family of backtests whose headline run (+13.6%/trade for the rule playbook vs +0.8%/trade for score-only filtering, reported 2026-10-14) we present alongside its subsequent re-runs (+1.8% to +12.5%/trade across windows) rather than behind them, and a short live verification window (swing: 96 closed trades, +5.34%/trade, 53.1% win rate — self-flagged below target). We document deliberate anti-lookahead and anti-survivorship mechanisms alongside residual leakage risks, and argue that evidence-gated self-improvement logs — accept/reject/revert decisions with their evidence — are themselves a useful research artifact for evaluating LLM-in-theloop trading systems.

detail.abstract: The development of decentralised finance (DeFi) challenges traditional compliance frameworks, which have historically relied on identifiable financial intermediaries, regulated institutions and clearly allocated responsibilities. By distributing financial functions among protocols, smart contracts, developers, governance participants and technical service providers, DeFi disrupts the institutional foundations upon which conventional compliance obligations are built. This article examines the extent to which the European Union's regulatory framework can address these challenges. It first analyses the difficulties arising from the decentralisation of financial functions and the identification of persons or entities subject to compliance obligations. It then considers the European Union's sectoral approach, particularly under Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 on Markets in Crypto-assets (MiCAR), and its limitations in addressing fully decentralised activities. Finally, it examines the specific risks associated with DeFi, distinguishing between endogenous risks arising from blockchain infrastructures, software and smart contracts, and exogenous risks resulting from dependence on external data and technological service providers. It argues that effective compliance in DeFi requires a shift from an exclusively entity-based approach towards a hybrid model combining legal accountability, functional analysis and technological risk management. In this context, programmable compliance may offer new preventive and monitoring mechanisms, although technological automation cannot replace legal responsibility or institutional supervision.

detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of Germany's July 2026 replacement of Bürgergeld (Citizen's Benefit)—a means-tested incomesupport scheme—with a more stringent successor within the same social assistance system, this paper asks whether a guaranteed income entitlement that makes it materially possible to refuse employment-related requirements also strengthens workers' power within employment relationships. Drawing on Italian operaismo, labor process analysis, and recent cash-transfer experiments, it distinguishes three frequently conflated effects: individual control over one's time, bargaining power vis-à-vis employers, and collective countervailing power. Panzieri, Alquati, and Tronti conceptualize wage labor as a contested social relation and labor struggles as potential drivers of capitalist reorganization. This perspective does not, however, directly establish a normative entitlement to any particular transfer system. Guaranteed minimum income (GMI) is therefore understood as a right to material security that requires an independent justification; removing employment-availability requirements is an institutionally testable proposition. The relevant counterfactual is an adequate, readily accessible means-tested support scheme with limited work-related obligations. Randomized transfer experiments in Germany, the United States, and Finland, along with an evaluation of Ireland's arts program, report varying effects on employment, time use, and health, but do not demonstrate automatic improvements in job quality or collective power. The paper develops an institutional comparison and identifies testable implications for voluntary exits, autonomy over time, workplace conditions, and collective organizing, while distinguishing benefit levels, behavioral conditions, and access costs. Material security can expand the feasible range of individual action; enduring countervailing power additionally requires collective organization, public services, and enforceable labor rights.

detail.abstract:
"This report presents findings from a second mapping exercise of social dialogue and collective bargaining experiences within the platform economy in Europe. It provides a descriptive analysis of various initiatives, offering an overview of key stakeholders, the main issues under discussion, notable developments and the emerging trends.

Building on the previous mapping exercise, which highlighted both the empirical and the legal barriers to social dialogue, as well as emerging best practice, this second comes at a pivotal moment. Since that first study, published by the European Trade Union Institute in 2023, key social policy instruments have been introduced at European level, notably the Platform Work Directive (PWD) and the competition law Guidelines, both of which have significantly reshaped the regulatory landscape. In parallel, several Member States have enacted national reforms which, in some cases, could be considered anticipatory transpositions of key provisions from the PWD.

Against this backdrop, with the PWD currently in its transposition phase, this updated mapping is especially timely. Developments in social dialogue can provide insights on how the Directive is being implemented across the EU, particularly in terms of its collective ambitions. It offers an overview of the changing social dialogue landscape and how this is evolving in response to recent regulatory changes. By pinpointing structural inconsistencies and gaps, the mapping helps predict the challenges that need to be addressed to ensure that the Directive’s collective dimension fulfils its potential and brings meaningful improvements for platform workers."

detail.abstract: A two-dimensional Itô diffusion with non-degenerate diffusion matrix is a Riemannian surface whose metric is the inverse of that matrix. For the SABR model this surface is the Poincaré half-plane, its curvature is minus the square of the volatility of volatility. The Hagan function, x(ζ), is the geodesic distance from today's state to the strike line, up to that same factor. This note develops the corresponding theory for several coupled SABR models and for options on baskets and spreads. The state space of n coupled models is a solvable Lie group with a left-invariant metric, correlation changes only a constant inner product on its Lie algebra. We give closed-form curvatures, the normal form in which the backbone correlations are gauge, and the embedded single-model planes. For baskets, we give the co-area version of the heat-kernel representation of the density, the leading-order implied volatility as moneyness over geodesic distance to the exercise hypersurface. Furthermore, the order-T coefficient away from the money, the at-the-money expansion to high order, the at-the-money level, skew and curvature of the leading smile in closed form, and the order-T 2 coefficient are given. Numerical results are supplied for stated parameter sets.

detail.abstract: Fitting each expiry of an implied-volatility surface and constructing a martingale coupling of the fitted marginals afterwards solves two problems in the wrong order: the fitted marginals need not admit a coupling of the intended kind, and the vanilla surface does not determine which coupling prices path-dependent contracts. We instead calibrate the joint law applying finite mixture models of Gaussian, resp. LogNormal type instead. A mixture component, or cell, carries a component forward (the level) and a component total variance. On a fixed dictionary of cells the vanilla fit, the normalisation and a conditional-mean condition on the cell transitions are linear in the weights and the transition masses, so the joint calibration is one linear programme. Every feasible point defines an explicit price martingale with exactly the fitted marginals. Its augmented state, the price together with the mixture cell, is Markov, while the price alone need not be. Feasibility is therefore a constructive sufficient guarantee that the marginals increase in convex order. The latter is not necessary and an explicit two-component marginals in convex order that no admissible pair attains on any dictionary containing their cells is constructed. Due to modelling choice, the transition kernel, every conditional law and the extremal couplings for a given payoff within the class are explicit. The vanilla surface leaves the coupling, and with it every path-dependent price, underdetermined, and the construction makes this measurable rather than hidden. For forward-start options, locally capped cliquets, Bermudan and American options we report class ranges and model-free martingale transport ranges separately. Class ranges are narrower because of the modelling restriction. They are ranges of the model class, not tighter no-arbitrage bounds. The non-identification goes beyond the vanillas: a one-parameter memory dial preserves every marginal and every joint law of two consecutive quoted dates. Yet it can be applied to move Bermudan put prices within the price interval, e.g. to achive a close match to a local-volatility value on the same vanillas. On a listed single-stock American chain the class reprices the European call quotes inside the spread. With the discount curve fitted to the same American puts, its early-exercise premium fits the put cross-section in sample better than a specified flat-volatility benchmark. The example establishes feasibility and comparative in-sample fit, not out-of-sample performance, and the coupling again remains unidentified.

detail.abstract: Contingent valuation (CV) and discrete choice experiments (DCE) measure the same Hicksian surplus and should in principle produce the same result. Whether they do, and under what conditions, remains a central question. We assemble 60 within-study comparisons from 40 environmental valuation studies that satisfy an explicit four-condition comparability rule. Although DCE produce higher willingness to pay (WTP) than CV in 60% of the comparisons (geometric mean WTP DCE-to-CV ratio = 1.20), the two methods agree more closely than individual studies imply. 75.0% of the comparisons differ by less than a factor of two, and 48.3% by less than a factor of 1.5. None of the study characteristics proposed to explain divergence (respondent overlap, number of attributes or choice tasks, efficient design, publication year) robustly predicts its magnitude or direction. Minimum detectable effects indicate that moderate associations would have been detectable for several of them. One design feature is consistently associated with less divergence: a DCE presenting a single experimentally varied alternative alongside the status quo. This is the DCE configuration closest to the referendum question in CV, and the multiplicative gap is about one third smaller. The association is stable in sign and magnitude across estimators and influence checks and remains distinguishable from zero under wild-cluster bootstrap inference, although it is exploratory and rests on five studies. Incentive-compatibility devices do not reduce the gap. Divergence between DCE and CV appears to be associated less with the elicitation method itself than with the cognitive task respondents are asked to perform.

detail.abstract: This paper asks when momentum thrives and which macroeconomic forces account for its long-run variation. Using a newly assembled monthly dataset covering more than 150 years of UK equity returns, we show that momentum persists across radically different market environments, but varies systematically with domestic business cycles and external geopolitical risk. detail.abstract: Using administrative firm-level data from Sweden, we document a robust asymmetry between debt maturity and firms' real adjustment: employment adjustment is substantially more closely associated with shortterm debt, whereas capital adjustment is more closely associated with long-term debt. The same distinction appears in firms' longer-run evolution: as firms age and become more capital intensive, their debt portfolios shift toward longer maturities. We develop a dynamic heterogeneous-firm model in which employment, capital, and debt composition are jointly determined. Short-term debt provides a flexible source of within-period finance but is exposed to default risk and priced endogenously, while long-term debt is collateralized by capital, costly to adjust, and carried forward on the firm's balance sheet. These differences make short-term finance particularly responsive to current operating needs and long-term finance closely tied to capital and collateral capacity. The calibrated model reproduces the debt-factor asymmetry in both levels and adjustment rates, as well as the joint increase in capital intensity and long-term borrowing over the firm life cycle. A policy experiment that guarantees short-term creditor recovery shows that selectively making short-term finance cheaper can substantially reallocate firms' debt portfolios while lowering capital and output, highlighting that the maturity composition of corporate debt matters for the real effects of credit-support policies.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether fiscal balances or broad-money growth better explain inflation in Syria over 1990–2024. These findings suggest that fiscal imbalances deserve greater attention in explaining Syria’s historical inflation, consistent with fiscal-dominance mechanisms, although neither causality nor the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level is established. Looking forward, effective economic reconstruction requires greater fiscal transparency, explicit reporting of public liabilities and their financing, reliable monetary statistics, and systematic evaluation of policy forecasts. Stronger institutional data and more credible fiscal–monetary coordination should therefore be priorities for future stabilization and research.

detail.abstract: Contested tribunal decisions are often cited as evidence that valuers disagree. This paper tests that reading against one tribunal's complete published output in one field: every decision of the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) in compensation, compulsory purchase and rating with a neutral citation between 2009 and 2026, as served by the Find Case Law collection of The National Archives — 380 of the 1,504 decisions the chamber handed down. On that test, 164 decisions (43%) were contests between valuations, a share stable across three periods. The other 216 turned on whether the claim could proceed at all (68), a question of law or fact with no figure in dispute (49), a value with only one valuation before the tribunal (42), whether a loss was compensable at all (35), and costs (22). A blind re-classification of 37 randomly sampled decisions agreed on 33. The findings describe the decisions read, not all valuation disputes. They suggest that much of what reaches the tribunal is not a disagreement between valuations, and that a report's most useful property in a contested matter may be handing the decision-maker a clean question.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remember past stock prices, so a backtest run on months a model has read can look like skill. We ask whether they remember Indian prices as well as US prices of comparable firms. detail.abstract: Accounting standard changes often refine classification precision-the reliability with which amounts appear in the correct account-without changing the reported total. Using an analytical model, I show that classification precision matters to investors when a firm has multiple activities that could be misclassified as one another and a capital structure with heterogeneous claims to cash flows. In the model, a firm must refinance debt after it reports; if it cannot, it defaults, the debt converts into equity at a deadweight cost, and the firm loses the tax deduction on its interest. When multiple accounts differ in persistence, more precise classification spreads investors' conditional expectation of the firm's terminal cash flow. Because default is costly, this spreading of beliefs decreases the value of a firm if and only if the firm's probability of default is below a threshold set by the risk-free rate alone. The face value of debt issued, cost of debt, and the equity value, however, can increase or decrease with classification precision. Extending the model to a costly persuasion setting, I show that a manager chooses greater classification precision only if the firm's probability of default is above the same threshold and greater classification precision is cheap. Greater classification precision also makes the equity prices of these firms more responsive to the reporting announcements. The model yields five empirically testable predictions.

detail.abstract: Traditional algorithmic market-making models suffer from severe performance decay due to non-stationary market regimes, where static parameters optimized for mean-reverting conditions frequently lead to inventory accumulation, adverse selection, and steep drawdowns during volatile or directional trends. This paper proposes a dynamic, regime-aware market-making framework that combines out-of-sample Walk-Forward Optimization (WFO) with a Reinforcement Learning (RL) meta-controller. We evaluate three foundational market-making paradigms: the classical Avellaneda-Stoikov model, an Inventory-Volatility-Adjusted model, and a Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading (VPIN) hedging model designed to detect order flow toxicity. To capture true market friction, parameter decay is mapped via WFO under strict inventory capacity limits, order-sizing bounds, and exchange transaction fees across six distinct structural regimes (high/low volatility, bullish/bearish, and high/low liquidity). The resulting out-of-sample execution logs serve as the foundational state-space for a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent, which functions as a micro-level meta-controller to dynamically reallocate continuous capital across the underlying algorithms in real time. Empirical evaluation on high-frequency, tick-by-tick order book data demonstrates that the WFO-PPO meta-architecture effectively mitigates adverse selection, stabilizes inventory skew, and reduces performance decay relative to monolithic models, providing a robust operational framework for quantitative execution in high-frequency trading environments.

detail.abstract: The Central Bank of Iraq sells dollars to banks and describes the sales as financing for imports. I ask what sets the volume sold: the oil dollars the state earns, the budget, or imports, with imports measured independently of the Bank from its trading partners' customs records. The oil inflow is rejected: sales are a stable share of spending and of imports (coefficients of variation 0.13 and 0.12) but not of the Ministry of Finance's dollar sales (0.27), and the ratio of sales to that inflow rises with the deficit. Imports and the budget both matter and are not separable in levels. In quarterly growth, sales rise 0.4 percent per percent of spending with imports held fixed, under controls for the market premium and regime breaks; at annual frequency the direct effect is not well determined, and about three-quarters of the budget's pull runs through imports. The dollars that imports do not account for rise by 14 to 24 cents per extra dollar of dinar spending, with or without the United Arab Emirates' re-exports in the import measure. Since 2017 the Bank's own import record follows its sales, not the goods its partners report. In 2026 the Ministry's dollar sales fell by four-fifths while spending held; the Bank kept selling, financed the budget with credit, and lost $18 billion of non-gold reserves.

detail.abstract: Structural-demographic theory (SDT) describes a cycle of order and disorder whose intensity varies sharply across societies at different states of economic development. This essay argues that whether a society is trapped in that oscillation or is spared it depends on its state of economic development, and that economic development is itself a process best understood through ecological succession. In succession, a stable environment lets a biological community grow ever more complex, while repeated disturbance (fire, flood, drought) holds it at a simple state. The division of labor runs the same course: left undisturbed it deepens from self-sufficiency toward a complete division of labor, and the volatility of grain output is the disturbance imposed on that process. Among societies of comparable endowment, then, how complex a division of labor can grow turns on how stable grain output is. Where volatility is high, prices are unreliable, a complete division of labor cannot be sustained, and society is locked into a shallow division of labor and violent oscillation. Where volatility is low, whether given by nature (northwest Europe) or produced by engineering (China), the division of labor accumulates continuously, industrialization follows, and society is spared the oscillation. How SDT plays out across civilizations, and the transformation of traditional societies into modern ones, thus come down to one measurable control parameter: the volatility of grain output, which by way of social structure shapes the interaction among commoners, elites and the state, and so provides the binding constraint on SDT.

detail.abstract: The transnational development and deployment of artificial intelligence have intensified longstanding questions concerning the territorial limits of national regulatory authority. AI systems are increasingly designed, supplied, operated, and relied upon across multiple jurisdictions, creating complex relationships among providers, deployers, intermediaries, public authorities, and affected individuals. This Article examines how international law constrains and informs the exercise of national regulatory power in this environment. It argues that technological interdependence does not eliminate territorial sovereignty, nor does the cross-border reach of AI systems establish an unlimited basis for extraterritorial regulation. Rather, the legitimacy of national regulatory measures must be assessed through established principles of jurisdiction, State responsibility, and international cooperation. Through a comparative examination of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act, the decentralized regulatory framework of the United States, and selected regulatory developments in New York, the Article identifies the legal and institutional tensions arising from divergent national approaches. It further examines the attribution of conduct involving autonomous systems to states, the continuing application of international humanitarian law to military and security uses of AI, and the limitations of contractual arrangements in allocating legal responsibility. The Article argues that market influence must be distinguished from jurisdiction, technical control from legal attribution, and regulatory compliance from the fulfillment of international obligations. It concludes that regulatory interoperability, rather than legislative uniformity or regulatory hegemony, offers a more sustainable approach to cross-border AI governance. Such an approach should facilitate compatible standards, conditional mutual recognition, and supervisory cooperation while preserving the legal independence of states and the international rules governing the exercise of public authority.

detail.abstract: Social disorder may erupt when markets unsettle customary obligations and formal institutions struggle to contain disputes. We study how commercialization and legal institutions shaped witchcraft accusations in early modern Scotland. Exploiting differential exposure to export price changes, we find more recorded accusations in better-connected places when prices were high. In these places, rents were more often paid in cash, with accusations more often following disputes over debts and trade. Furthermore, accusations more often entered judicial proceedings but less often ended in recorded guilty verdicts. Formal law had opposing effects, with deed registration dampening the response and adjudicatory capacity amplifying it. After the Privy Council restricted prosecution in 1662, the earlier positive association between commercialization and accusations was no longer apparent.These findings suggest that commercial pressures can turn local grievances into persecution, with the extent of escalation shaped by how the state organizes and constrains local legal authority.

detail.abstract:
We develop three extensions of the adjoint kernel-sensitivity theory for the rough Heston characteristic exponent. The starting point is the Volterra--Riccati functional
\[
\LT(K,g;z)=\int_0^T F\bigl(z,\psi_K(T-r,z)\bigr)g(r)\,\dd r,
\]
where the Riccati state is driven by the memory kernel \(K\). The original sensitivity theory perturbs \(K\) while holding the input curve \(g\) fixed. We first derive the corresponding sensitivity formula when the forward variance curve \(\xi(t)=\mathbb E[V_t]\) is held fixed instead. Since \(g=\xi+\lambda K*\xi\), a kernel perturbation \(h\) induces the additional input perturbation \(\delta g=\lambda h*\xi\). This yields an explicit corrected sensitivity density \(B_K^\xi\), obtained from the original adjoint density by a direct integral correction and requiring no additional adjoint equation.

Second, we replace the first-order approximation diagnostic for a multi-factor kernel by an exact path identity. Along the admissible segment \(K_\varepsilon=(1-\varepsilon)K_M+\varepsilon K_H\), the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the exact characteristic-exponent difference as the integral of the forward-variance-preserving sensitivity along the path. This identity has no Taylor remainder constant. It also leads to a practical quadrature-based validation protocol in which the adjoint is recomputed at a small number of path points and the resulting prediction is compared with an independently computed fractional-Riccati solution. We explain why a relative comparison against a single small reference indicator can be misleading and propose scale-stable alternatives.

Third, we differentiate along the fractional-kernel family \(H\mapsto K_H\). The map is continuously differentiable into \(L^1(0,T)\) for \(H>0\), with
\[
\partial_H K_H(t)=K_H(t)\bigl(\log t-\digammafn(H+\tfrac12)\bigr).
\]
Combining this derivative with the adjoint representation gives a chain rule for \(H\mapsto \LT(K_H,g_H;z)\). In the forward-variance-preserving regime, the formula simplifies to a single pairing with \(B_{K_H}^\xi\). In the classical fixed-\((V_0,\theta)\) parametrization, it instead contains the explicit derivative of the input curve. These formulas provide a common framework for comparing kernel sensitivity with expansions in the Hurst parameter, including the expansion studied by Hager and Kreher.

The results are analytical identities and a numerical research programme; no new numerical values are claimed here. The purpose is to turn the original first-order diagnostic into a verifiable error analysis and to distinguish clearly between fixed-input and fixed-forward-variance perturbations.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the daily risk of Arafura Rare Earths (ASX: ARU), a pre-production rare-earth developer, between August 2018 and June 2025. I therefore find no exploitable departure from weak-form efficiency. What is predictable is risk. I fit AR(1)-GARCH and EGARCH models with Normal, Student-t and skewed-t innovations, and a GARCH model with Poisson jumps, and evaluate their one-day Value-at-Risk forecasts out of sample for long and short positions. The decisive modelling choice is the shape of the innovation distribution rather than the volatility recursion. detail.abstract: I examine short-term liquidity shocks as a determinant of housing instability among low-income households. To do this, I exploit the PATH Act that, starting in 2017, delayed Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) refunds by several weeks without affecting eligibility or refund amounts. These findings establish short-term liquidity shocks as a cause of eviction and EITC timing as a driver of eviction seasonality. This suggests that policies targeting short-term liquidity can reduce housing instability.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how relief from households' business debt affects the allocation of their labor using large-scale agricultural debt relief programs in India. Existing research on such programs presents a puzzle: despite substantial debt forgiveness, farm investment and productivity do not improve. I offer a potential explanation: households may respond to debt relief by reallocating labor across economic activities, generating benefits beyond the indebted farm that conventional farm-level evaluations miss. I exploit quasi-random eligibility cutoffs in two large debt relief programs and use administrative bank records linked to business registries. Relative to comparable ineligible households, relief-eligible households reduce their reliance on urban wage work, which some of their members pursued by migrating temporarily to cities. Survey evidence suggests that these migrants return home. The same households increase small-business borrowing and start more non-farm businesses in their home districts, shifting labor from urban wage work toward local non-farm entrepreneurship. The evidence is consistent with relief reducing the need for predictable wage earnings and easing constraints on entrepreneurial risk-taking. More exposed districts also see greater business formation and economic activity. Business debt relief thus shapes household labor allocation well beyond the indebted enterprise.

detail.abstract: What explains politicians’ climate attitudes? Using complete sets of congressional tweets and medium-and-large cities' directly elected mayors’ tweets, several fine-tuned large language models, and a measure of city governments’ flood adaptation effort, I find evidence that city governments' flood adaptation effort reduced nearby cities' mayors’ expressed belief in climate change science and reduced their expressed support for climate change mitigation policies; this evidence is consistent with an income effect. On the contrary, local governments’ flood adaptation effort led to increases both in the representing US House members’ expressed belief in climate change science and in their support for climate change mitigation policies. The evidence suggests that politicians see mitigation policies as nonexcludable goods: during the several years after a climate disaster, politicians seek to shift the cost of reducing similar future disasters to other constituencies while decreasing support for local effort to reduce these disasters.

detail.abstract: Some European competition authorities have recently argued that immunity recipients require stronger protection from private damages liability in order to preserve incentives to report cartels. In Buccirossi et al. (2020), we show that this concern is well founded: the perceived conflict between effective leniency programmes and compensation for cartel victims is not inherent, but results from the way civil liability is allocated. We compare two forms of protection. Full immunity from civil liability maximises deterrence but may reduce compensation when the remaining cartel members cannot satisfy the claims. The former "Hungarian solution" instead makes the non-reporting cartel members pay first while retaining the immunity recipient as a residual source of recovery. This paper focuses on the latter allocation, the deterrence-maximising allocation subject to preserving recoverable compensation, which we call liability of last resort. We clarify two misunderstandings in the subsequent debate. First, reducing the immunity recipient's expected payment need not reduce victims' ability to recover compensation: the recipient remains liable for any shortfall. Second, damages paid in detected cases are not a complete measure of consumer protection. Stronger reporting incentives can reveal hidden cartels and facilitate claims against the remaining infringers, while earlier detection and deterrence can prevent consumer harm altogether. Recent declines in leniency applications and cartel investigations have brought renewed attention to these issues. The optimality of the liability of last resort solution, however, does not depend on those trends or their causes: it strengthens deterrence without sacrificing recoverable compensation.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms are changing how firms design, coordinate, and govern operations by integrating artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital sensing and digital twins, data infrastructure, and additive manufacturing. This paper develops a selective research agenda for production and operations management by distinguishing enabling technologies from the platforms, workflows, and business models through which they are deployed. We organize the agenda around a common sequence linking technological capability, operational manifestation, mechanism, outcomes, and boundary conditions. The relevant mechanisms include prediction, information visibility, verification, orchestration, monitoring, human override, and decision rights. We articulate how these mechanisms may create operational value through improvements in productivity, quality, responsiveness, resilience, compliance, and customer experience, enabling firms to capture financial value through revenue growth, cost reduction, risk avoidance, and improved asset utilization. We first identify enduring operations management themes that emerging technologies may reshape. We then develop five forward-looking paths involving artificial intelligence-enabled business-tobusiness platforms, physical-digital integration, agentic service workflows, data and artificial intelligence governance, and platform-enabled resilience under geopolitical disruption. Finally, we discuss theoretical and methodological approaches that can support cumulative research.

detail.abstract: The European Union's Omnibus I package substantially simplified the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) before firms had begun implementing its original requirements, creating a distinctive case of anticipatory regulatory reform. We examine how this reduction in regulatory ambition is likely to affect multinational enterprises (MNEs), focusing on four major amendments: the reduced number of companies in scope, the introduction of a value chain cap, the removal of harmonized civil liability, and the elimination of the requirement to implement climate transition plans. detail.abstract: Organisations invest heavily in leadership development, yet the return on that investment is difficult to demonstrate. This paper examines what research says about the effectiveness of leadership development programmes and how their value can be evaluated. Using an integrative narrative review of leadership training research and evaluation frameworks, combined with a qualitative analysis of two publicly documented cases (General Electric's Crotonville leadership development centre and Google's Project Oxygen), the paper addresses three research questions about programme effectiveness, the design features and evaluation methods that distinguish strong programmes, and the benefits and risks visible in practice. The synthesis indicates that leadership training can be effective when it is based on a needs analysis, includes practice and feedback, and is supported by the organisation, but that many programmes fail because of weak design, poor transfer, and inadequate evaluation. The cases show that programmes aligned with strategy and built on evidence about what effective leaders actually do are more likely to produce a measurable return. The paper concludes with recommendations for designing and assessing programmes.

detail.abstract: This article examines why growth in Latin American economies has not uniformly translated into a sustained reduction in economic gaps. An integrative review and historical comparison of Brazil, Chile, Costa Rica, Mexico, and Uruguay, with South Korea as a contrasting case and the United States as a benchmark, connect institutional debates with evidence on structural change, learning, and informality. The contribution is a conceptual synthesis distinguishing access, absorption, and persistence that guides case-specific questions. The design is descriptive, and the selected countries do not statistically represent the region. The reviewed evidence suggests that broadening and sustaining productive capabilities helps translate sectoral advances into persistent catch-up.

detail.abstract: Economic and social researchers often infer detailed distributions from incomplete observations. Entropy-based methods can select coherent reconstructions, but the assumptions that make a solution unique need not identify the properties needed for an empirical claim. This methodological perspective distinguishes observed information, identification, distribution selection, validation, and claim-relative interpretation. detail.abstract: The appointment of women as Heads of the Office of Religious Affairs (KUA) in 2026 marks a crucial milestone in the history of Indonesia's religious bureaucracy. Data sources are drawn from statutory regulations, policy documents from the Ministry of Religious Affairs, and scholarly literature on the merit system, representative bureaucracy, and gender equality. These findings confirm that meritocracy and gender equality are not conflicting concepts; rather, they operate synergistically to support the transformation of a professional, public-service-oriented religious bureaucracy.

detail.abstract:
In today's competitive global economy, U.S. companies upholding strict labor and human rights standards increasingly face unfair competition from unscrupulous foreign firms that exploit forced labor. In this Essay, we argue that this exploitation is not just a grave human rights crisis but also a serious market distortion that disadvantages ethical businesses in the United States and elsewhere. 

This Essay outlines a strategic approach to confront this unfairly uneven playing field. Beyond simply deploying the existing legal tools, we propose a unified federal enforcement strategy and smarter trade agreements with enforceable labor standards. We also propose affirmative incentives, including procurement preferences and legal safe harbors, for companies that invest in ethical sourcing. The final component to the integrated strategy we propose is greater investment in traceability technologies and public-private partnerships to identify and root out forced labor deep within supply chains. Ultimately, we outline a forward-looking blueprint to ensure fair and competitive markets for U.S. businesses, ones that reward integrity and drive a global race to the top in labor practices. Economic competitiveness and human dignity, we argue, must be pursued together, not treated as competing priorities.

detail.abstract: Disagreement is the cornerstone of the capital markets, for if all agreed on what a share of stock was worth, few would buy or sell it. Some have predicted that generative artificial intelligence (AI) will give rise to an "algorithmic monoculture" as investors increasingly rely on a small number of large language models (LLMs) trained on the same underlying data. We test that prediction in a pre-registered study of how six open-weight LLMs forecast earnings per share (EPS) from 8,476 SEC filings made after the models' training cutoffs. Model forecasts are far more dispersed than analysts' forecasts. Against analysts who issued or reconfirmed a forecast within ten trading days after the filing, the cross-model standard deviation is 5.7 times larger (geometric mean). The models' revisions in response to the same filing are 8.9 times more dispersed than analysts' revisions. But most of this disagreement is not informed. When each model is queried repeatedly, more than 90% of the variance in the panel's answers is sampling noise within a model rather than disagreement between models. Replacing the filing with a random scramble of its words changes cross-model dispersion by only 16%, and the scrambled filing yields forecasts about as accurate as the real one. Model revisions move toward the realized number only 36% of the time, against 62% for analysts, and model dispersion does not reliably predict trading volume or returns. Model errors are also less correlated with each other than analysts' errors, although most of that difference disappears once sampling noise is averaged out, and the models share a common optimistic bias. What separates the models is mostly which information they select, not how they interpret it: when each model forecasts from the others' summaries of a filing, the summarizer explains about half of the variance and the forecaster about an eighth. Under this protocol, LLMs do not form a belief monoculture; they produce disagreement that is large but mostly noise. We discuss what this means for investor protection, the "reasonable investor," and fraud-on-the-market

detail.abstract: Leading AI developers have adopted unusual legal structures to show that safety will not be traded for profit. These include public benefit corporations, controlling foundations, special classes of shares, purpose trusts, safety committees and published safety frameworks. This article argues that such structural safeguards share a common weakness: each can be lawfully undone, renegotiated, reinterpreted, outlasted or sidestepped, and few people have standing to object. Because regulators, courts and the public rely on them, the safeguards are worth less than the reliance placed on them. I call this shortfall the reliance gap. The prevailing regulatory model, which trusts developers to write their own commitments and verifies compliance with whatever those commitments currently say, does not close the gap, because it measures conduct against a text the developer remains free to rewrite. The gap is most serious where the people exposed to risk include those not yet born, because the value of a promise over a long horizon depends on its durability rather than its present strength. The article makes three contributions. First, drawing on the legal form of atomic energy control, it shows that the last technology of comparable stakes was governed by public licence rather than private promise. Second, it offers a typology of eight lawful routes by which a corporate safeguard can be reversed, each illustrated from primary documents. Third, it proposes a stricter regime, with a reform matched to each route, built on existing models of public approval, statutory representation and oneway commitment, and reinforced by proactive supervision and public-interest litigation.

detail.abstract: Look-ahead leakage arises when a forecasting model incorporates information that would not have been observable at the time the forecast was generated. Chronological splits and purged cross-validation cannot detect leakage embedded within the feature construction process itself. We introduce a straightforward audit: a feature is point-in-time valid only if recomputing it on data truncated at any given moment leaves all preceding values unchanged. This truncation test is complemented by a perturbation test and clock audits, which delineate five classes of leakage. In simulations without directional predictability, and in five years of one-minute data from seven European equity indices, leaky features inflated directional accuracy to as high as 0.90, transforming a loss-making model into one that appears consistently profitable in backtesting. Several widely adopted Python library functions fail the audit. In a production system, the audits uncovered two instances of feature leakage and two data faults in datasets previously considered corrected.

detail.abstract: How does data regulation reshape organizational boundaries in the age of AI? We study this question in the context of AI startups. AI startups typically license the latest general-purpose AI models to develop their products. They can tailor the licensed model with additional data and changed parameters or leave this standardized input unadapted, and they can let customers tailor the product with their own data. Either choice carries a cost. Tailoring the model and holding proprietary data in-house reduce dependence on upstream model providers and can make the product more differentiated. However, these adaptations expose the startup to greater liability. The contracts startups use to access models and training data are often incomplete. How a model learns from updates and added training data is a black box, so responsibility for any potential harms a product may cause is difficult to assign. We find that AI startups reporting GDPR-related data deletion are more likely to source LLMs externally and to offer products that customers can tailor with their own data, yet they develop more of the surrounding technology stack in-house. Using panel variation since 2020, we also find that reported data deletion is associated with lower fundraising, concentrated among Europe-exposed startups. These findings suggest that liability from regulatory exposure raises the net cost of holding residual control rights, a cost that the property-rights view of the firm has not considered.

detail.abstract: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.

detail.abstract:
Most investors do not read mutual fund disclosures, yet disclosure remains the central regulatory tool of U.S. securities law. This gap between regulatory design and investor behavior has led many scholars to conclude that disclosure is largely ineffective. This Article shows why that conclusion is wrong.

Drawing on original interviews with investment advisers, fund managers, compliance officers, and fund counsel, we demonstrate that the principal consumer-protection effects of disclosure occur before any document reaches the public. The process of drafting, reviewing, and revising mandated disclosures activates professional norms, legal oversight, and organizational routines that shape how mutual funds design products, market shares, manage portfolios, and comply with the law. Across institutions, disclosure operates as a powerful private-The governance mechanism organized around a simple norm: “Say what you do and do what you say.”

By revealing the hidden work of disclosure, the Article reframes decades of skeptical scholarship and offers a more accurate account of how modern securities regulation protects the more than 128 million Americans who invest in mutual funds to finance retirement, education, and long-term financial security. Our argument has particular urgency in an era of administrative atrophy, as reduced enforcement capacity has intensified calls to weaken, if not abandon, disclosure-based regulation. Reconceptualizing disclosure as a form of co-regulation that mobilizes private governance inside firms, the Article explains why disclosure may continue to protect investors ex ante even as public oversight weakens. More broadly, the Article offers regulatory design principles for leveraging private governance to protect consumers in complex, information-dense markets.

detail.abstract: We study a portfolio transfer learning problem in which an investor combines portfolios learned from different markets to invest in a new market. Since data scarcity in the new market makes it difficult to estimate optimal combination weights, we study why the simple yet competitive equal weighting approach can be effective and whether it can be further improved. We provide a robust optimization justification for deterministic equal weighting (DEW), showing that it is nearly optimal among deterministic robust combinations when distributional uncertainty is sufficiently large and its worst-case expected return is positive. We further show that randomization can improve the worst-case performance of DEW. Specifically, we establish conditions under which uniform randomized equal weighting (UREW), which randomly selects a candidate portfolio while maintaining equal combination weights in expectation, outperforms every deterministic combination. This improvement is explained by the tradeoff between market-specific risk efficiency and diversification benefits. Finally, we develop an algorithm to optimize the randomization distribution. By construction, the optimized randomized equal weighting achieves a worst-case expected Sharpe ratio at least as high as those of DEW and UREW. We establish finite-sample Sharpe ratio guarantees for the proposed equal weighting methods. Numerical experiments demonstrate their competitive worst-case and out-of-sample performance.

detail.abstract: How will artificial intelligence transform work and jobs, and for whose benefit? This paper argues that the answer depends on how AI is organized and governed. Drawing on neo-Schumpeterian research, I situate AI as a new phase of the digital revolution and examine how earlier technological revolutions generated changes in management models and societal institutions. This history reveals opportunities for broadly shared prosperity, but no guarantee that they will be realized. To clarify AI's diverse workplace effects, I distinguish two dimensions commonly conflated in debates about automation and augmentation: the substantive complexity of human work and the enabling or coercive character of managerial control. I argue that public policy helps determine the prevalence of these four types of work. I then distinguish four policy regimes according to their public planning capacity and the extent of citizen and worker participation. I argue for combining stronger public capacity with consequential participation to steer AI development and deployment, protect employment transitions, support skilled and rewarding work, and distribute productivity gains more widely.

Trade secrets, proprietary software, and unregistered designs can hold substantial commercial value, yet their use in debt financing is complicated by the absence of public title registries. This comparative study examines how these assets can support financing across the United States, European Union, China, and Japan, with additional perspectives from the United Kingdom and Singapore.

The analysis distinguishes three requirements: legal protection, enforceable security, and practical recovery following default. It examines how verifiable digital evidence, including blockchain anchoring, trusted timestamps, and confidential storage, can help lenders assess asset history, ownership records, continued protection, and changes to the collateral. Such evidence supports due diligence but does not itself create rights, perfect security interests, or establish recoverable value.

Across differing legal frameworks, the financing opportunity depends on the rights a company can offer, the income those rights generate, and their usefulness to a potential acquirer. The paper translates these findings into three illustrative financing scenarios and an operational evidence dossier for innovators and credit underwriters.

detail.abstract: The deep integration of software and hardware in smart products creates a pronounced datacollection advantage: the developer can leverage equipment-generated data (EGD) to iteratively refine algorithms and enhance hardware-software synergy. These improvements, however, depend on whether the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) shares EGD with the developer. When access is restricted, a developer lacking data may instead manufacture hardware devices to collect data independently. We develop a game-theoretic model to examine the interaction between the OEM's data-sharing policy and the developer's hardware market entry under data-driven learning. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, the developer enters the hardware market when its relative hardware quality is sufficiently high, and the OEM can deter such entry by voluntarily sharing EGD. Interestingly, stronger data-learning capability increases the developer's entry incentive when the OEM withholds EGD but reduces this incentive when the OEM shares EGD. Second, although data-driven software updates enhance value creation, the OEM may optimally withhold EGD when the developer's relative hardware quality is moderate. By doing so, the OEM sacrifices part of the learning benefit but induces the developer to enter the hardware market as a weaker rival, thereby lowering the software licensing fee. Third, stronger data-learning capability may induce the OEM to switch strategically from sharing to withholding EGD, which benefits the OEM and hurts the developer but can also benefit consumers. Overall, our study offers actionable guidance on how firms can balance data collaboration against channel conflict in technology supply chains.

detail.abstract: Numerous studies have examined mechanisms for eliciting consumers' willingness to pay (WTP) for products. However, a consumer's "absolute" valuation differs from their "relative" WTP, and their reported values depend on whether they are myopic or sophisticated. How can these quantities be accurately elicited in a single interaction? We propose a BDM-CMV hybrid mechanism that elicits both valuation and WTP from myopic consumers and WTP from sophisticated consumers. The mechanism also guarantees incentive compatibility for myopic consumers and approximate incentive compatibility for sophisticated consumers.
